_comment: QUESTIONS THE CROSS-SECTOR LADDER RAISED AND DID NOT ANSWER, brief 11.
A RUNG TEST IS FROZEN (D-B1, re-anchored at D-A1) AND A PROPOSED CHANGE TO ONE
COMES HERE. That is the whole purpose of this file: the pass that scores an
instrument is the worst possible pass to loosen it in, because a rung that scores
badly looks like a defect in the rung and may only be a finding.
A READING OF A TEST IS NOT A CHANGE TO IT and goes in scope.md under the frozen
test — which unit a sector's owners state, which input edge rung 6 is about. The
line between the two is what several of these questions are about.

questions.question: Does rung 2 ask a question CO2 storage and transport operators answer?
questions.what_the_table_shows: 6 of 102 scored entries clear rung 2 — the lowest rate of any rung in any sector, and an order of magnitude below cement's 20 of 42 off the same publisher's list.
questions.why_it_may_not_be_the_projects: A capture plant has a nameplate and its owner states it. A PIPELINE is a route and a STORE is a reservoir, and what an operator publishes about either is a licence area, a first-phase injection rate, or nothing. The IEA's own file carries a capacity column for these rows and this register does not read capacity off a benchmark (D82), so the only source is the owner, and the owner is often silent by the nature of the asset rather than by reticence.
questions.the_proposal_that_is_not_made_here: That rung 2 admit a stated STORAGE CAPACITY in Mt, as against a rate in Mt a year, for this sector. It is not made because it would change what the rung asks in one sector and not another, and a rung that means different things per sector cannot be compared across them — which is the entire point of the cross-sector table.
questions.what_would_settle_it: A reading of the 96 entries that fail: if most state a total capacity and no rate, the rung is asking the wrong unit. If most state nothing at all, 6 of 102 is a finding about the sector.

questions.question: When a funder's list is READ and names no participant, is rung 4 `fail` or `unread` for the entries it would have covered?
questions.what_happened: The two battery IPCEIs — SA.54793 and EuBatIn SA.55855 — are EUR 6.1 billion of approved State aid to 59 companies in twelve Member States, and the Commission's own page for them NAMES NOT ONE COMPANY. The participant infographics are .zip archives; the decisions are PDFs at competition-cases that yield no participant list. The four HYDROGEN IPCEIs publish readable participant infographics and brief 12 scored rung 4 from them.
questions.why_it_matters: Six battery entries clear rung 4, all from the Innovation Fund. If the battery IPCEIs were readable the number would very likely be higher, and every battery `fail` on rung 4 is therefore a fail measured against a smaller set of funder lists than hydrogen's — the two columns of the cross-sector table are not measuring quite the same thing.
questions.how_this_pass_handled_it: The programme is recorded in sources/funder_pass.json with `outcome: READ AND NOT ENUMERABLE`, and no battery entry is scored pass OR fail from it. The rung 4 fails stand on the Innovation Fund's list, which IS enumerable, so they are fails against a list that was read — which satisfies D-L2 — and this question records that the list is not all the lists there are.
questions.the_proposal_that_is_not_made_here: A fourth cell state, `partially searched`, or a per-entry record of WHICH funder lists covered it. Both are changes to what a rung records and neither is made in the pass that would benefit from them.

questions.question: Not a rule question. A coverage question, recorded so a reader does not mistake a gap in brief 9 for a finding about two sectors.
questions.what_the_table_shows: Rung 6 is `not_searched` on 34 of 42 scored cement entries and 97 of 102 in transport and storage. The dependency sweep of brief 9 recorded an owner side for 117 projects: all 66 hydrogen rows, 32 of 33 battery rows, all 8 steel rows — and 8 of 34 cement rows and 3 of 43 transport-and-storage rows.
questions.why_it_is_here: `not_searched` is the honest cell and it is also nearly the whole column. A reader scanning the cross-sector table sees 2 of 42 and 0 of 102 and will read it as two sectors with no contracted inputs. THE RIGHT READING IS THAT NOBODY HAS LOOKED, which is a fact about this register.
questions.what_would_settle_it: A dependency sweep over the 26 cement and 40 transport-and-storage rows brief 9 did not reach. That is work, not a ruling, and it is queued rather than argued.

questions.question: Should a pass rate be reported for a sector where two thirds of the population is refused by the perimeter?
questions.what_the_table_shows: Steel's population is 147 and 98 of them are perimeter exclusions — scrap EAFs and works with no announced route change, refused after their owners were read. 49 entries are scored. Hydrogen refuses 53 of 245; cement refuses none of 42.
questions.why_it_is_here: D-L1 already settled that an exclusion is not scored, and the denominator is therefore right. The question is different: the five columns of the cross-sector table have denominators that mean very different things, because each sector's list was drawn by a publisher with its own idea of what belongs in it. GEM lists every steel plant at 0.5 mtpa and above; the IEA's cement rows are all capture projects by construction. A COLUMN IS NOT A SECTOR, IT IS A LIST.
questions.the_proposal_that_is_not_made_here: Reporting pass rates over admitted rows only, which would make the columns comparable and would throw away the whole point of scoring the list rather than the register.
questions.what_this_pass_does: Prints the population, the scored count and the excluded count under every column, so the denominator is never read without the refusals beside it.

questions.question: Does rung 4 record that an award WAS made, or that it stands?
questions.what_happened: Four of the 33 awards matched in this pass carry the funder's own status TERMINATED: Giga Arctic (Freyr, Mo i Rana, EUR 100m), ANRAV (Devnya, EUR 189.7m) and the HYBRIT demonstration (LKAB, EUR 143m), which names two works and so counts twice.
questions.the_precedent: D-B10 ruled on exactly this shape for Catalina in brief 12: the fiche says TERMINATED, the pass prints it in the queue and does not write it, and rung 4 passes on the award. This pass follows that without re-arguing it.
questions.why_it_is_still_a_question: Four in 33 is not one in 55. Rung 4 reads 'a funder publishes an award naming the project', and a funder publishing that it has ENDED an award is the same funder publishing about the same project with better information. A rung that counts the award and ignores the termination is recording the past tense of a fact the same document corrects.
questions.the_proposal_that_is_not_made_here: That rung 4 fail on a terminated award, or that it gain a second cell for the award's current state. Either is a change to a frozen test and neither is made in the pass that found the four.

questions.question: Not a rule question. A finding recorded so the number is not misread.
questions.what_the_table_shows: Steel clears rung 1 on 18 of 49 scored entries — the lowest of the five sectors, where every other sector clears it on more than half.
questions.why_it_is_here: The steel population is keyed by WORKS, and GEM's own row already names the works and its municipality. What rung 1 asks is whether THE OWNER OR THE PERMITTING AUTHORITY names the site, and GEM is neither. So a works everybody can find on a map fails rung 1 when its owner has published nothing about the project — which is the rung working exactly as written, and looks like a register that cannot locate steel plants.
questions.what_would_settle_it: Nothing. It is recorded because the cross-sector table invites the comparison and the comparison is misleading without this sentence.

questions.question: Should a citation whose every fetch record is a refusal fail the build?
questions.what_was_confirmed: THE CITATION GATE DID NOT MATCH BYTE FOR BYTE AND NOW MEASURES IT. check_citations.py asked whether a cited URL appears in a fetch index — a STRING comparison — and it walked only data/transition/projects.json and technologies.json. Two changes: the five census files are walked now, which is where the twelve truncated URLs of D-S12 lived and why no gate saw them; and sources/check_citation_bodies.py asks the stronger question, whether a body exists under the hash the index records.
questions.what_it_found: 441 distinct citations checked against the bytes in six caches: 118 have a body on file, 28 are hand-read and filed, 30 were fetched and every record is a refusal, and 238 are in no index on this machine.
questions.why_it_is_not_blocking_yet: A CACHE IS PER-WORKTREE AND GITIGNORED. A body fetched in the main checkout is absent in the census checkout, so 'no bytes here' can mean the citation is bad or that the bytes are one directory over, and this gate cannot tell those apart. A gate that blocks on the difference blocks on where somebody is standing. AND IT IS MID-PASS: the standing rule of 21 September is that no rule changes until brief 14 and the supplier sweep are in.
questions.what_would_settle_it: Run it in the main worktree, where the hydrogen bodies are, and see how many of the 57 survive. If most do, they are real defects and the gate should block; if most resolve, the gate needs to read every worktree's cache or the caches need to be one shared store.
questions.note_on_the_list: The gate prints the first thirty; the count is 57. Run it for the whole list.
questions.ruled: 2026-09-21. Reporting only, as written. BEFORE THE PAPER'S TABLE IS CALLED FINAL, run check_citation_bodies in both worktrees and print the union; every citation must show a body, a hand-read copy, or a refusal somewhere. No gate blocks on which directory a session stands in.

questions.question: Two entries classed `searched none found` have an owner page that names the works. Do they move, and to what?
questions.why_held: THE STANDING RULE OF 21 SEPTEMBER: nothing is amended mid-pass, and a case the rules do not settle goes here with the entry held. These two are not rule questions — the rules settle them — but the pass that found them is the pass that would benefit from them, which is the shape D-B1 froze the rung tests against. They are written with the evidence so the next pass classes them rather than re-finding them.

entries.verbatim: Press release 2026-09-10: 'Volvo Group announces energy park initiative as next step in Mariestad. Volvo Group announces next step in the Mariestad expansion process with plans for an energy park near the intended battery cell production site.'
entries.reading: THE OWNER NAMES THE SITE and calls the cell plant 'intended'. That clears the site leg and leaves the capacity leg unstated, so the class it supports is `named not admitted`, failed leg CAPACITY — not an admission. `searched none found` is wrong either way: something was found.

entries.verbatim: The front page carries 'Dunkirk Gigafactory Groundbreaking' twice, in its own carousel.
entries.reading: THE OWNER NAMES THE WORKS AND SAYS IT HAS BROKEN GROUND. A carousel caption is thin for an admission and it is not nothing: the class it supports is at least `named not admitted`, and a deeper read of prologium.com is the task.

questions.confirmed_not_changes: FOUR MORE WERE READ AND DO NOT MOVE, which is worth recording because they look like hits in the signal column. EAS Nordhausen, BMZ Karlstein and BASQUEVOLT Vitoria-Gasteiz all match on the place name IN THE IMPRINT — which is exactly what the battery census already recorded as the failure ('bmz-group.com names Karlstein am Main exactly once, in the imprint'). Holcim's Carboneras match is a photo exhibition, 'Carboneras en fotos'. AND iea:1662's owner host is barseback.com, WHICH IS A GOLF RESORT — a bad host in the earlier record, not a finding about the Barsebäck Hydrogen Hub.
questions.ruled: 2026-09-21. Both reclassed through the normal path to `named not admitted`, failed leg CAPACITY, each with the original class named as a search miss. sources/ladder_docket.md, D-A22.

questions.question: Fifteen hydrogen entries are classed `searched, none found` on domains this register invented from the project's name. What are they classed instead?
questions.what_the_record_shows: QUOTED FROM sources/research_pass_14_summary.json, key `the_admission_search_guessed_domains`. The admission search of 10 September ran over 167 entries and gave every one the same four EU press URLs, then for most of them `<projectname>.com` and `<projectname>.eu`. In 47 entries EVERY non-EU host it tried was derived from the project's own name. www.labskive.com for Green Lab Skive, www.castellon.com for BP's Castellón refinery, www.ccuaalborg.com for the Green CCU Hub at Aalborg — and www.barseback.com for the Barsebäck Hydrogen Hub, WHICH IS A GOLF RESORT.
questions.why_it_is_not_simply_wrong: THE GUESS IS OFTEN RIGHT, which is how it survived: 28 of the 47 came back `owner or permit source names the site`, because a project frequently is at its own name. A guessed domain that answers and names the works is a fact, however it was reached. What cannot stand is the other column.
questions.the_problem: For these fifteen, `searched, none found` rests on domains nobody published. A guessed domain that 404s is not a search, and the class says the register looked where the owner is. IT DID NOT LOOK ANYWHERE THE OWNER SAID IT WAS.
questions.what_would_settle_it: A fourth outcome in the admission search's own vocabulary — `no owner domain located` — separating 'the owner's pages say nothing' from 'no owner page was found'. That is a change to a census's class vocabulary and the standing rule of 21 September holds it until brief 14 and the supplier sweep are in.
questions.and_it_is_not_this_pass_s_mistake_alone: BRIEF 14's OWN SEARCH INHERITED THE GUESSES. research_pass.py takes an entry's owner host from the hosts in its own records and refuses to invent one — and the records it read already contained invented hosts, so twelve of the eighty-two entries in the browser queue are queued against a domain that never existed. The rule against folding a name into a key is only as good as the records it reads.
questions.ruled: 2026-09-21. A domain is never derived from a project's name. Every search record states how the owner's host was established and check_search_records.py gates it. The 11 confirmed-by-content guesses keep their result with the provenance recorded; the 20 whose verdict rested on unconfirmed guesses reopen as not_searched and were searched by a recorded query. D-A21.
questions.correction: THE FIGURES IN THIS QUESTION AND IN #74 WERE WRONG. 47/28/15 came from a substring test that counted endesa.com as derived from 'Huelva - Endesa'. Re-measured on the shape the search generated — two or more hosts sharing a stem across TLDs — the figures are 60 / 11 / 20.

questions.question: One cited URL has a fetch record that is not a refusal and no bytes on any machine here. Does a citation whose body was not kept still count as read, and on what evidence?
questions.what_the_record_shows: D-A25's union of `check_citation_bodies.py` over both worktrees on the paper-freeze commit leaves exactly one citation in the CITED AND NEVER READ class: https://api.iea.org/hydrogen/project, cited at data/transition/projects.json.projects[75].disagreements[0].speakers[1] — the IEA's 104 MW_input figure for BayH2 against the company's 128 MW. sources/cache/hydrogen/index.json holds one record for it: 2026-09-09, 496,671 bytes, outcome `fetched 2026-09-09 by build_hydrogen_benchmark.fetch()`. The body is under no sha in any of the four worktrees' caches.
questions.why_it_is_not_simply_wrong: IT IS NOT A REFUSAL AND NOT A GAP IN THE SEARCH. The document was fetched, the reading is what the benchmark file is made of, and the register's own drift and disagreement machinery has been reading IEA ref 1221 out of it since. What is missing is the COPY, and the copies are gitignored by design — `dep_restore.py` exists because this repository has always held that the index is the tracked claim and the bytes are a convenience.
questions.why_it_was_not_cleared_before_the_tag: A FETCH TODAY WOULD NOT BE EVIDENCE OF THE 9 SEPTEMBER READING. api.iea.org serves the current vintage; filing today's bytes under that URL would put a different document behind a dated disagreement and make the citation look checked when what had been checked is something else. So it is listed rather than cleared, and the paper's table carries it as the single open citation.
questions.what_would_settle_it: Either a rule that an index record naming a byte count and a date is sufficient evidence of reading where the body is absent — which is close to what check_citations already does with its 2026-09-15 baseline — or a restore path that keeps one copy of a benchmark blob per vintage, which is a decision about what the cache is for and not a fix to this row.
